Cy Quadri

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: split the four corners of a shape, and the places where the split lines meet always sit on one circle.
How to play: Drag the corners A, B, C and D, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Choose inside or outside splits, show the angle marks, or press Reset.
Bisectors
Look for the math

Move any corner of a four-sided shape and the drawing changes completely, yet four new points still land on a single circle. Here is why, and why it works for the lines outside the shape too.

What the old page claims

The explanation says:

“Angle bisectors in a quadrilateral form another quadrilateral which is cyclic, i.e. a quadrilateral that can be inscribed in a circle. Indeed, the sum of opposite angles of the latter is always 180°. The same holds true for the external angle bisectors.”

The live article now shows a GeoGebra picture instead of the Java applet. A 2007 capture of the same page still embeds CyQuadri with exactly three choices: “Internal bisectors”, “External bisectors” and “Show angles”. Those are the options on this page, and the construction below follows the applet's bytecode. There is no winning move: this is a picture to explore.

Four halves, four crossings

At each corner, the applet halves the angle between the two neighbouring sides. The point where the halves from A and B meet, the one from B and C, the one from C and D, and the one from D and A become the corners of the new shape. The green circle is drawn through the first three of them. Choosing “External bisectors” turns each half-line by a right angle before drawing; it does not change the four original corners. These are angle bisectors of the four corners themselves, not of angles made by diagonals.

Why the opposite angles add to 180°

Write the four angles of the starting shape as A + B + C + D = 360°. In the triangle made by side AB and the two inside half-lines, the crossing angle is 180° − (A + B)/2. At the opposite crossing it is 180° − (C + D)/2. Adding the two gives 360° − (A + B + C + D)/2 = 180°, which is exactly the test for a cyclic quadrilateral. For the outside half-lines each small angle at a corner is 90° − A/2, so the crossing angles become (A + B)/2 and (C + D)/2, and these also add to 180°. The fourth crossing therefore lies on the circumcircle drawn from the other three.

What the check found, and the other applet

The logic test repeats the applet's own arithmetic a second time and compares it on thousands of shapes in both modes. It finds the four crossings on one circle every time, including shapes that are dented or crossed; the largest circle error is below 0.00001 board units. The “180°” sentence is about ordinary convex shapes: there the angle sums agree too. A dented or crossed shape can have a reflex angle, so an unsigned angle measurement no longer describes the quadrilateral in the usual way, though the circle still does. This is not the sibling CyclicQuadrilateral applet: that one starts with four points on a circle and halves its arcs to make incenters and a rectangle; here four freely dragged corners work just as well.

Try the outside half-lines, then drag one corner far away: the circle grows and moves, but the four crossings stay on it.
